title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) intervention increases the fraction of validator‑passing vendor‑specific CLI configurations produced from operator intent, relative to direct LLM generation. Tasks were a curated multi‑vendor (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) intent manifest; a deterministic validator encoded syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic routing‑reachability, and destructive‑pattern checks; and the model was gpt-5-mini. Per the preregistered paired design, a single initial candidate was generated per task and shared between the baseline (no repair) and guarded (validate + single automatic repair if validator fails) arms. Across 300 paired tasks the initial candidates passed the deterministic validator in every case (baseline success rate = 1.00; guarded = 1.00; n11=300; n10=n01=n00=0). The paired difference was 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.00; 95% CI 0.00–0.00). We report the full preregistration, deterministic validator rules, task manifest, provider traces, and analysis artifacts. The null result shows that, for this manifest and model snapshot, the G‑V‑R pipeline provided no measurable additional safety benefit because the initial generation already satisfied the deterministic operational checks. We discuss practical interpretations, constructive uses for guarded pipelines despite ceiling effects, threats to validity (task design limits, single‑model evaluation, validator coverage), and reproducibility artifacts to enable independent follow‑up.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, runbook generation, and automated remediation. Operators typically deploy guardrails (validators, simulators, repair loops) to reduce operational risk. Prior work has proposed generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) and tool‑augmented LLM pipelines to improve correctness and operational safety, but quantitative, preregistered evidence measuring the incremental safety benefit of G‑V‑R in realistic multi‑vendor CLI synthesis is limited and often confounded by dataset and evaluation differences. Research question and contribution. We ask: to what extent does a deterministic‑validator‑centered G‑V‑R pipeline increase the probability that a generated vendor CLI fragment passes operational validation, relative to direct LLM generation? Contributions: (1) a machine‑readable preregistration and a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor intent manifest published with provenance; (2) a deterministic validator implementing operationally meaningful checks and a paired confirmatory execution across 300 tasks using gpt-5-mini under a strict shared‑initial‑candidate protocol; (3) full execution artifacts and a transparent analysis showing no measurable benefit from the G‑V‑R intervention for this manifest and model, and a discussion of implications and limitations.
sections.related_work: LLM→NetOps translation and intent‑based configuration: prior studies have explored fine‑tuning, in‑context learning, and RAG for mapping intents to vendor CLI (e.g., Nguyen Tu et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2024; Mondal et al., 2025). Benchmarks and evaluation frameworks (NetLLMBench, 2024) emphasize task diversity and validator design. Work on formal or SMT‑based BGP and network policy verification (Weitz et al., 2016; Bagpipe) motivates deterministic validators and soundness concerns. Recent surveys of LLM‑AIOps and agentic NetOps highlight the need for rigorous, reproducible evaluation of operational safety mechanisms. We position this study as a tightly preregistered, artifact‑anchored confirmatory test focused on the marginal safety contribution of a single‑repair G‑V‑R policy when initial generations are shared between arms.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. We preregistered study_id study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e and froze the experimental plan (see preregistration SHA‑256 a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). Design: within‑task paired binary outcomes (success if validator accepts a candidate within the per‑arm model‑call budget). Sampling: curated 300 tasks covering typical operational intents (VLAN migration, MTU changes, uplink switchover) across Cisco IOS, JunOS, and Arista, with deterministic seeds. Intervention arms: baseline — single initial generation per task (shared candidate); guarded — validate the same initial candidate, and if it fails, allow one automatic repair generation and re‑validate. Model and prompts. Model declared: gpt-5-mini (execution snapshot recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). A single preregistered vendor‑adapter prompt template produced the shared initial candidate; the repair prompt template and canonicalization rules were fixed and published in the Docker artifact. Validator. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements: (a) syntactic parsing for vendor CLI fragments, (b) interface assignment and allowed‑field invariants, (c) workflow ordering constraints (e.g., shut→modify→no‑touch patterns), (d) simple reachability‑style invariants and forbidden destructive patterns (e.g., take both uplinks down). The validator is deterministic, rule‑based, and exercised on normalized configurations. Execution and logging. Per preregistration, each task produced one initial model call (shared). Baseline outcome = validator(initial_candidate). Guarded outcome = validator(initial_candidate) OR validator(repair_candidate) if repair was invoked. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, seeds, and hashes were recorded and published. Analysis plan. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: two‑sided exact McNemar (paired) with 95% CI (paired bootstrap percentile implemented per preregistration). Secondary analyses: per‑vendor paired tests with Bonferroni correction and exploratory repair diagnostics (repair success conditional on initial failure). Missingness and contamination. Predefined retry policy handled transient provider failures; contamination detection (exact/fuzzy match and high‑entropy token heuristics) was implemented and logged. All decisions and artifacts are in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution summary. The run completed per preregistration: 300 paired tasks, 600 planned episodes, 600 completed episodes, 300 model calls used (only the shared initial generation stage invoked), zero failed episodes. Primary outcome. Every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator: baseline_success_count=300 (1.00), guarded_success_count=300 (1.00). Contingency counts: n11=300, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired estimate: paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap resamples=10,000; seed 1729). Secondary and exploratory outcomes. There were no initial validator failures; consequently no repair calls were made and repair diagnostics are vacuous for single‑repair policy. Per‑vendor paired comparisons are identical (no discordant pairs). Execution artifacts. Full raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, task manifest, and analysis artifacts (contingency tables, condition summaries, reproducible analysis log) are published and hash‑signed (see manuscript_evidence_bundle/artifact list).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The confirmatory test found no incremental safety benefit from the preregistered single‑repair G‑V‑R policy because the initial generation already satisfied the deterministic operational checks in every case. This null result has three non‑exclusive explanations: (1) ceiling‑effect: for this manifest and model snapshot the initial generator reached the validator’s decision boundary (all pass), leaving no room for improvement; (2) validator scope: the deterministic checks, while operationally meaningful, are a conservative subset of real‑world execution hazards (they do not model dynamic stateful interactions, timing, or deep routing correctness); (3) model quality and prompt design: the chosen model snapshot and vendor prompt produced high‑quality vendor CLI fragments for the curated intents. Practical implications. A guarded G‑V‑R pipeline remains valuable in broader settings where initial generation fails deterministic checks or when validators include richer dynamic/simulation checks; our results do not imply guarded pipelines are unnecessary generally. Instead, they highlight that the marginal utility of guarded repairs depends strongly on task difficulty, validator coverage, and model capability. Reproducible follow‑ups can (a) raise validator granularity (add emulated execution or Batfish‑style checks), (b) expand task diversity and adversarial cases, and (c) vary model snapshots/sizes to observe regime changes. Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared‑initial‑candidate design was deliberate (preregistered) to isolate repair effect but also ensures identical starting points; no post‑hoc changes were made. Construct validity: the deterministic validator operationalizes a subset of 'non‑harmful' properties—omitted hazards reduce generality. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini) and a synthetic but operationally informed 300‑task manifest limit generalizability across models, prompts, and production complexity. Conclusion validity: the observed perfect baseline outcome leads to zero discordance and exact inference (p=1.00) but precludes estimating positive improvement under the chosen design; power calculations in the preregistration assumed nonzero discordance. Recommended next steps. To measure G‑V‑R benefit empirically: (1) include intentionally adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents; (2) broaden validator coverage toward dynamic/simulation checks; (3) test multiple model snapshots to sample varying generator quality; (4) consider repeated‑repair policies or bounded iterative repair when initial failure rates are nontrivial.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, paired confirmatory study to quantify the marginal safety benefit of a deterministic single‑repair G‑V‑R pipeline for vendor CLI generation. With gpt-5-mini and our curated 300‑task manifest, the initial shared candidate passed the deterministic validator in all tasks; consequently the guarded pipeline produced no measurable improvement. The result underscores that (a) the added value of guarded repair depends on initial generator error rates and validator expressiveness and (b) preregistered, artifact‑rich evaluations are essential to avoid misleading inferences about safety mechanisms' efficacy. We publish all artifacts to enable follow‑up studies that vary task hardness, validator fidelity, and model families to map the regimes where G‑V‑R meaningfully reduces operational risk.

The agentic orchestration framework and exact prompt templates used for generation and repair are included in the published Docker artifact (execution/model_configuration.json and execution/provider_calls/*).
limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic, interface invariants, workflow ordering, forbidden destructive patterns) and omits dynamic/simulation checks and deep routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or real‑world out‑of‑distribution failure modes; manifest design produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) intentionally isolates repair effect but prevents measurement of generation variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; multi‑iteration repair policies were not tested.
Potential model memorization/contamination cannot be eliminated entirely by heuristics; contamination detection artifacts and sensitivity analyses are provided.
